Customer interested in reserved GPUs for low-latency inference, strict data isolation (VPC/on-prem considerations), burst capacity for peak trading windows, and predictable cost. Security team present with SOC2/KMS/audit log questions. Agreed to run a pilot benchmark and follow up with pricing and security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Tom R. (Head of ML, Sundown), Priya N. (Platform Eng), Carlos V. (CISO), Lina G. (Product)

Auto Summary: Sundown evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted. Main asks: reserved GPU pools, VPC + private control plane options, burst/bursting to hosted during peak, SLA for latency, audit logs and KMS integration.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Ethan our SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:05] Tom: Yep good, thanks. Tom here. We wanted to go through our workloads and see how dedicated looks like, especially around reserved GPUs and burst.
[00:10] Ethan: Cool, quick agenda, we can run through current infra, workload patterns, isolation/compliance, then sizing and a pilot. Sound good?
[00:18] Priya: Sounds good. We'll kick it off with our current stack - we productize a couple of LLM features for customer support and fraud detection, everything's in k8s on AWS, using spot nodes for inference today.
[00:28] Tom: Right now we're on a mix of open models hosted via a mixture of provider APIs and some in-house smaller models on EC2, but the latency and cost really vary. We're seeing big variance during market open spikes.
[00:40] Maya: Got it - and are you primarily evaluating Dedicated for cost predictability, data isolation, or latency SLAs?
[00:46] Tom: All three, honestly. Latency matters for fraud detection (P95 target about 120ms), cost predictability for budgeting, and we need isolation because we process payment card related metadata in some flows.
[00:58] Carlos: And on the security side we need SOC 2 compliance, KMS integration, audit logs and the ability to restrict egress. Also SAML SSO and RBAC for developers.
[01:10] Ethan: That fits well with Redwood Dedicated - we offer private control plane and VPC peering, plus KMS/HSM options. A few clarifications - when you say P95 120ms, is that for single-shot generation at ~512 tokens or for chat style where kv-cache matters?
[01:30] Tom: Mostly single-shot scoring calls, like prompt -> rerank -> decision, about 128-512 tokens. We also have some longer chat flows but less latency sensitive.
[01:40] Priya: Our peak QPS is spiky - baseline about 30 qps but peaks to ~400 during events for a 10-15 minute window. We were hoping for a burst strategy so we don't have to commit to huge reserved pools.
[01:55] Maya: We see that pattern a lot. Our Dedicated product supports reserved pools plus burst to hosted in some regions, and there's a config for guaranteed capacity + burst. We should detail the SLA differences between pure dedicated capacity and burst-to-hosted - latency SLAs are stricter on dedicated.
[02:12] Ethan: Also worth noting how batching and KV caching reduce cost; with a good prefix cache and batching we can reduce per-token cost but that can change latency distribution. For scoring calls with 128 tokens, continuous batching gives good throughput.
[02:28] Tom: Any ballpark on how many GPUs we should reserve for baseline vs burst? Our team measured a 95th percentile latency of ~200ms on current infra but variability is high.
[02:40] Ethan: Quick back-of-envelope - for 30 baseline qps with 128 tokens and gpt-like model, you'd likely be fine with 2-4 A100-equivalent GPUs depending on quantization and kernel optimizations. For 400 qps peak you'd need more - usually customers pair reserved baseline with burst capacity or autoscaling policies.
[02:58] Priya: We can't use unlimited autoscaling because budget approvals won't allow a huge commit. What about predictable burst caps?
[03:06] Maya: We offer burst quotas - you reserve baseline and buy a burst pool that you draw from during peaks; pricing differs for burst (higher unit cost) but you get cap control. Alternatively, policy-based overflow to hosted API is another pattern - that gives near-unlimited burst but comes with cross-product routing and slightly higher latency when routed.
[03:26] Carlos: How do you handle data residency and logs if overflow goes to hosted? We can't have sensitive payloads leaving our VPC.
[03:34] Ethan: Good callout. For overflow to hosted we'd recommend masking or sending only non-sensitive metadata. For fully sensitive workloads you can configure dedicated-only routes and a private control plane/on-prem stack. We also support network egress controls so logs don't leave your configured storage.
[03:52] Tom: For the scoring pipeline, we can't risk anything leaving the VPC unencrypted. Would Private deployment be required then?
[03:58] Maya: If the compliance bar requires no data to ever go to hosted endpoints, Private (VPC + private control plane) or on-prem is the safe route. Dedicated with VPC peering and customer-managed KMS is often sufficient if policies allow controlled egress.
[04:14] Priya: From a networking standpoint, we'll need detailed diagrams - how peering works, how the control plane talks to the serving plane, and whether we can run the control plane in our subnet.
[04:23] Ethan: We'll share an architecture diagram. Short answer: we can do a private control plane with VPC peering, and in some cases deploy a customer-managed control plane for higher isolation. We'll include that in the security packet.
[04:35] Lina: Quick question on model versioning and rollouts - can we pin model versions and do canary tests?
[04:40] Ethan: Yes, rollouts, canary, auto-fallback to previous model variants are supported. That folds into the Redwood Console for observability and per-route dashboards.
[04:50] Tom: For the pilot, we'd like to simulate our peak and run ~1k requests with our scoring prompts to see latency and throughput, and verify quantization impacts.
[04:59] Maya: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot plan - typically 2-4 weeks, with an initial benchmark on sample prompts. Ethan will scope the env and resource needs.
[05:10] Priya: Another ops question - what's the upgrade window for model or runtime changes? We need predictable maintenance windows.
[05:18] Ethan: Dedicated nodes have configurable maintenance windows; automatic kernel upgrades only happen in scheduled windows, and we provide rollback to previous runtime images if there's an issue.
[05:28] Carlos: On keys - KMS integration, can we bring our own key (BYOK) and restrict key usage per model/route?
[05:34] Maya: Yes, BYOK is supported in Dedicated and Private. You can scope keys to routes and retain audit logs. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the security packet.
[05:45] Tom: Pricing - what's the pricing model for reserved capacity vs burst vs pilot? We need monthly committed spend numbers to present to finance.
[05:53] Maya: Pricing for Dedicated is typically a reserved hourly GPU price based on commitment (monthly/annual), plus a management fee. Burst-to-hosted is metered at a higher per-token rate. For pilot we can provide a fixed short-term package. I'll send a pricing sheet.
[06:06] Ethan: One more technical nuance - quantized model variants can significantly reduce GPU memory and increase throughput; we'll recommend quantization where accuracy is acceptable, and we can test that in the pilot.
[06:18] Priya: Our ops team is also concerned about observability - token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and tracing.
[06:25] Ethan: Redwood Console has token-level cost and per-route dashboards, tracing hooks, and error analysis. We can turn on retention for deeper analysis; retention is an add-on.
[06:36] Tom: OK, good. On SLA, are there explicit latency SLAs or is it uptime only?
[06:41] Maya: We provide uptime SLAs and latency targets for Dedicated under enterprise contracts; we can include P95 latency targets in Dedicated SLAs but it depends on the committed config and region. We'll formalize that in the proposal.
[06:55] Carlos: We'll need SOC 2 Type II evidence, pen test reports, and details on audit logs and HSM usage.
[07:02] Maya: We'll attach the security packet; it includes SOC 2 attestations, pen test summary, audit log examples, and KMS/HSM notes.
[07:10] Priya: For the pilot, what access will we need to provide? VPC peering, sample data, and representative traffic pattern?
[07:18] Ethan: Exactly - we'll need VPC peering details or a controlled test VPC and a sample prompt set and traffic profile. We'll also need permission to deploy the serving runtime into the reserved pool.
[07:28] Tom: Do you support private registries for model artifacts? We host our models in a private artifact repo.
[07:33] Ethan: Yes, we support pulling models from private registries with authenticated access; we'll include the steps in the enablement doc.
[07:41] Lina: Any competitors we should be aware of? We've been talking to Anthropic and using OpenAI for hosted.
[07:46] Maya: Totally - we often see Anthropic and OpenAI for hosted use-cases; for Dedicated folks also look at AWS SageMaker or on-prem solutions like Paperspace. We'll highlight differentiators in the follow-up.
[07:58] Priya: One more latency question - is 120ms P95 feasible on dedicated A100-class hardware for our 128-token scoring?
[08:05] Ethan: It's realistic if you optimize models (quantization, kernels), use the right batch strategy, and keep KV cache warm. We'll validate during the pilot.
[08:14] Tom: Great. Let's talk timelines - we'd like to start a pilot in two weeks and decision by end of Q2.
[08:20] Maya: Two weeks is doable. We'll send pricing and security docs by EOD Friday and propose pilot scope early next week.
[08:28] Carlos: We'll circulate a list of compliance questions, but please mark anything that requires legal review.
[08:33] Maya: Will do. Ethan, anything to add?
[08:36] Ethan: I'll follow up with the pilot runbook and resource estimate. Expect specifics on GPU counts and test harness.
[08:44] Tom: Ok thanks everyone.
[08:46] Maya: Thanks - recap: Maya send pricing/security, Ethan send pilot plan, Sundown to share traffic profile and compliance questions. We'll schedule technical deep dive with Priya next week.
[08:58] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[09:00] Carlos: Bye.

(Notes: Transcription includes occasional mis-heard words and timing markers approximate; some proper nouns may be transcribed imperfectly.)
